title: Financial Crime Foundations for Regulatory Staff
summary: An eight-module foundation programme giving regulatory staff a grounding in AML/CFT, sanctions and fraud, firms' controls and financial crime red flags.
topic: Reducing Financial Crime & Delivering Market Integrity
intro: This training programme equips regulatory staff with a sound grounding in money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions and fraud, how firms' controls work and how to spot financial crime red flags in everyday supervisory work.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give regulatory staff a practical understanding of the main financial crime risks, the international framework set by the FATF and the controls firms are expected to operate. Participants leave able to recognise red flags in their own work, ask the right questions of firms and know when and how to escalate concerns, including to the national FIU.
sections.What It Covers: Money laundering and terrorist financing basics, the FATF framework and mutual evaluations, sanctions, fraud, how firms' controls work, red flags in supervisory work, working with the national FIU and law enforcement, and a red flags case workshop.
Intended Audience: New joiners and developing staff across supervisory, authorisation, policy and enforcement functions
Supervisors and inspectors without a specialist financial crime background
Staff joining a financial crime or AML/CFT supervision team
Learning Objectives: Explain the stages and methods of money laundering and terrorist financing
Describe the FATF standards and how they shape national frameworks and the authority's role
Explain how sanctions and fraud risks arise in financial firms
Describe the controls firms are expected to operate and how supervisors test them
Identify financial crime red flags in authorisation, supervisory and enforcement work
Apply appropriate escalation, including cooperation with the national FIU and law enforcement
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a four-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a short briefing with typologies, case studies and exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's mandate and sectors.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: No prior financial crime experience is required. Some familiarity with financial services or the authority's work is helpful.
Core Reading: FATF (2012, as updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2017, revised 2020), Sound Management of Risks Related to Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism
FATF (2023), Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons

modules.title: Understanding Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing
modules.summary: What money laundering and terrorist financing are, how they work in practice and why financial firms are both vulnerable to them and central to preventing them.
objectives: Explain the stages of money laundering and the sources of criminal proceeds
Distinguish terrorist and proliferation financing from money laundering
Recognise why the financial system is attractive to criminals
syllabus: Placement, layering and integration
Predicate offences and the scale of illicit finance
Terrorist financing and proliferation financing compared
The harm caused and the authority's role in preventing it

modules.title: The FATF Framework and the Authority's Role
modules.summary: The international AML/CFT standards set by the FATF, how they are implemented nationally and what they require of supervisors.
objectives: Describe the FATF Recommendations and the risk-based approach
Explain the authority's responsibilities as an AML/CFT supervisor
Recognise the importance of mutual evaluations and national risk assessments
syllabus: The FATF Recommendations, Immediate Outcomes and methodology
National risk assessments and the risk-based approach
Supervisory obligations: licensing, monitoring and sanctions
Mutual evaluations, follow-up and the consequences of grey-listing

modules.title: Financial Sanctions
modules.summary: How targeted financial sanctions work, the obligations they place on firms and the risks of breach and evasion.
objectives: Explain the purpose and types of financial sanctions
Describe firms' screening, freezing and reporting obligations
Recognise common sanctions evasion techniques
syllabus: International, regional and national sanctions regimes in outline
Asset freezes, prohibitions and ownership and control tests
Screening, alert handling and reporting obligations
Evasion: front companies, trade routes and crypto-assets

modules.title: Fraud and Scams
modules.summary: The main types of fraud affecting financial firms and their customers, how fraud links to money laundering and what firms should do to prevent and detect it.
objectives: Identify the main internal and external fraud types
Explain how authorised push payment fraud and investment scams operate
Assess firms' fraud prevention and detection arrangements
syllabus: Internal fraud, insider threat and misconduct
Investment scams, impersonation and authorised push payment fraud
Money mules and the link between fraud and laundering
Prevention, detection and customer protection measures

modules.title: How Firms' Financial Crime Controls Work
modules.summary: The building blocks of a firm's financial crime framework and what good and poor controls look like in practice.
objectives: Describe the main components of a firm's AML/CFT framework
Distinguish effective controls from paper compliance
Frame supervisory questions to test controls
syllabus: Business-wide risk assessment, policies and governance
Customer due diligence, beneficial ownership and enhanced due diligence
Transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting and record-keeping
The MLRO, compliance function, training and independent testing

modules.title: Red Flags in Supervisory Work
modules.summary: How financial crime risks surface in authorisation applications, supervisory reviews and firm data, and how staff outside specialist teams can spot them.
objectives: Recognise financial crime red flags in applications and firm information
Use data and returns to identify unusual patterns
Decide when concerns should be referred to specialist colleagues
syllabus: Red flags at the gateway: ownership, source of funds and business plans
Red flags in supervision: growth, customer base and geography
Unusual transactions, products and delivery channels
Escalation routes within the authority

modules.title: Working with the FIU and Law Enforcement
modules.summary: How the authority cooperates with the national FIU, law enforcement and foreign counterparts, and the legal and practical considerations involved.
objectives: Explain the role of the national FIU and how suspicious activity reports are used
Describe the gateways for domestic and international information exchange
Recognise the authority's own reporting and confidentiality obligations
syllabus: The FIU's functions: receipt, analysis and dissemination
Domestic cooperation and national coordination arrangements
International cooperation and memoranda of understanding
Tipping off, confidentiality and data protection

modules.title: Financial Crime Red Flags: Case Workshop
modules.summary: Brings the programme together in a case study in which participants review a firm's profile and information, identify financial crime risks and agree the supervisory response.
objectives: Identify financial crime risks and red flags in a case scenario
Assess the adequacy of the firm's controls
Agree and justify an appropriate supervisory response and escalation
syllabus: Case briefing: firm profile, customer base and transaction data
Identifying red flags and control weaknesses in small groups
Deciding on escalation and referral
Workshop: presenting findings and the proposed supervisory response

related.title: Crypto-Asset Financial Crime: Typologies, Tracing and Controls
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping supervisors, FIU analysts and investigators to recognise crypto-asset crime typologies, trace funds on-chain and assess service providers' controls.

related.title: Financial Crime Supervision in the Age of AI
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess financial crime controls and firms' use of AI in monitoring, screening, fraud and surveillance.

related.title: The EU AML Package: AMLR, AMLD6 and AMLA (EU Edition)
related.summary: An eight-module programme on the EU AML package for supervisors and firms: the AML Regulation single rulebook, AMLD6, AMLA's supervisory model, crypto-asset transfers and transition planning.

related.title: Asset Recovery: Tracing, Freezing and Confiscation
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping practitioners to trace, restrain, confiscate, manage and return criminal assets, including crypto-assets and assets held abroad.

related.title: Enforcement and Sanctions
related.summary: A ten-module programme taking enforcement and supervisory staff through the full life of an enforcement case, from triage and evidence to sanctions, settlement and cooperation.

related.title: Financial Investigation: Following the Money
related.summary: A ten-module programme equipping investigators and analysts to run parallel financial investigations, trace funds through accounts and corporate vehicles, and present financial evidence.
